required_facts.statement: Without ORDER BY, a query’s output order is unspecified.
ORDER BY column ASC sorts ascending and ORDER BY column DESC sorts descending; ASC is the default.
Write ORDER BY first_column ASC, second_column DESC to sort by the first column and break its ties with the second.
When not otherwise specified, NULL values sort last for ASC and first for DESC; NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST overrides that placement.

text.content: Suppose a reporting result contains North amount 100, South amount 100, and West amount 30. Without ORDER BY, its output order is unspecified. A stakeholder’s expectation that the biggest amounts appear first must be stated in the query.

text.title: SQL Sorting and Ordering Results
text.content: Without ORDER BY, a query’s output order is unspecified.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: ORDER BY column ASC sorts ascending and ORDER BY column DESC sorts descending; ASC is the default. Write ORDER BY first_column ASC, second_column DESC to sort by the first column and break its ties with the second. When not otherwise specified, NULL values sort last for ASC and first for DESC; NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST overrides that placement.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Write:
SELECT Branch, Amount FROM ReportRows ORDER BY Amount DESC, Branch ASC;

Amount DESC puts larger amounts first. Branch ASC breaks the 100 tie, so the example order is North, South, West. The second sort column matters only when the first values tie. ASC is the default when a direction is omitted.

For the SQL NULL-ordering convention used here, NULL values sort last with ASC and first with DESC unless overridden. To place missing amounts last in a descending report, use:
SELECT Branch, Amount FROM ReportRows ORDER BY Amount DESC NULLS LAST, Branch ASC;

If an East row has NULL Amount, that explicit placement puts it after the non-NULL amounts. Treat the stated default as the documented SQL behavior used here, not a universal assertion about every database engine.

The practical result is an ordering rule a report reader can understand: primary comparison, direction, tie-breaker, and where missing values belong. A consistent-looking order in one earlier result is not a substitute for specifying it.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Observed output order is not a guarantee without ORDER BY. Also, descending does not automatically put NULL last under the documented default here. State NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST when the report needs explicit placement.

practice_anchor.objective: Write a query selecting Branch and Amount from ReportRows, sorting Amount descending and breaking equal-amount ties with Branch ascending.
practice_anchor.success: The query uses ORDER BY Amount DESC, Branch ASC and returns North 100, South 100, then West 30.

live_code.required_skill: Apply a primary sort direction and a secondary tie-breaker direction in ORDER BY.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide ReportRows with columns Branch and Amount and rows West 30, South 100, and North 100, alongside an editable SELECT Branch, Amount FROM ReportRows; statement.
live_code.observable_success: The completed query specifies Amount DESC before Branch ASC; its result places North before South because their amounts tie, and places West last.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show ReportRows beside its ordered result, making the descending Amount comparison and ascending Branch tie-breaker visible. Include a separate East row with NULL Amount to contrast the documented descending default with explicit NULLS LAST.

notes: NULL defaults are source/dialect-specific; do not generalize them to all SQL engines.

required_facts.statement: For a top-N report, compute the metric per group, order it descending, and limit the output: SELECT group_column, SUM(value_column) AS total FROM table_name GROUP BY group_column ORDER BY total DESC, group_column LIMIT n;
source_refs: postgres_docs#https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html — 7.2.3 — The GROUP BY and HAVING Clauses

required_facts.statement: A predictable limited result requires an ordering that determines which rows come first.
LAG(metric) OVER (ORDER BY period_column) retrieves the previous row’s metric for an ordered period comparison; the first row has NULL by default.
SUM(metric) OVER (ORDER BY period_column ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) computes an ordered running total over the rows through the current row.

text.title: Business Reporting Query Patterns
text.content: For a top-N report, compute the metric per group, order it descending, and limit the output: SELECT group_column, SUM(value_column) AS total FROM table_name GROUP BY group_column ORDER BY total DESC, group_column LIMIT n;

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: A predictable limited result requires an ordering that determines which rows come first. LAG(metric) OVER (ORDER BY period_column) retrieves the previous row’s metric for an ordered period comparison; the first row has NULL by default. SUM(metric) OVER (ORDER BY period_column ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) computes an ordered running total over the rows through the current row.

text.title: A business analysis example
Keep the distinction clear
text.content: LIMIT alone does not determine which rows come first. LAG retrieves the previous ordered row, while the specified SUM frame accumulates rows through the current one. Do not describe these distinct calculations as if they all simply return a grouped total.

required_facts.statement: In Power BI Desktop, Home > Get data selects a connector and connects to a data source.
Choose Transform Data to open Power Query Editor and shape the data before loading it.
Change a column’s data type and remove unnecessary columns using the editor’s column commands; the transformations are recorded as applied steps.
Use Close & Apply to apply the transformations and load the shaped data.

text.content: Imagine receiving a dispatch-orders source with OrderID, Amount, and an unnecessary note column. You need to connect and shape the data before loading it into Power BI Desktop, and Amount should have a type appropriate to its numeric information.

text.title: Power BI Data Import and Transformation
text.content: In Power BI Desktop, Home > Get data selects a connector and connects to a data source.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Choose Transform Data to open Power Query Editor and shape the data before loading it. Change a column’s data type and remove unnecessary columns using the editor’s column commands; the transformations are recorded as applied steps. Use Close & Apply to apply the transformations and load the shaped data.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Use Home > Get data to select the connector and connect to the source. Choose Transform Data to open Power Query Editor. There, use column commands to change Amount’s data type and remove the note column that is unnecessary for this example. The transformations are recorded as applied steps.

Inspect the intended shape before loading: the example needs the order identifier and amount, with the correct type for Amount. The applied steps record the transformations rather than requiring you to describe them only from memory. Then use Close & Apply to apply the changes and load the shaped data.

The practical distinction is between connecting to a source and shaping the data before loading. The path teaches tool use from scratch, so keep the connector, editor, and final apply action explicit. This example does not yet create relationships, measures, or report visuals. Its output is loaded, shaped data for later work, not a completed dashboard merely because a connection succeeded.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Get data is the connection step, not the whole transformation workflow. Transform Data opens the editor, and Close & Apply applies and loads the shaped result. Recorded applied steps are transformations, not a substitute for checking the intended columns and types.

practice_anchor.objective: Connect to the supplied dispatch-orders dataset containing OrderID, Amount, and an unnecessary note column using Home > Get data. notes: Do not introduce DAX, BI relationships, or report canvas commands.

required_facts.statement: Select a connector in Tableau’s Connect pane and provide the source-specific connection information.
To create a physical join, drag the first table to the canvas, double-click it, then drag another table into that join canvas.
Select the join type and matching fields in the join dialog; inner keeps matches, left or right preserves its named side, and full outer preserves both sides.
An extract is a saved snapshot of data for analysis; select Extract on the Data Source page and configure the extract before saving it.

text.content: Suppose a hypothetical Tableau report needs Customers and Orders from a source. Start in the Connect pane, choose the appropriate connector, and provide that source’s connection information. Connection details depend on the selected source.

text.title: Tableau Data Connection and Preparation
text.content: Select a connector in Tableau’s Connect pane and provide the source-specific connection information.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: To create a physical join, drag the first table to the canvas, double-click it, then drag another table into that join canvas. Select the join type and matching fields in the join dialog; inner keeps matches, left or right preserves its named side, and full outer preserves both sides. An extract is a saved snapshot of data for analysis; select Extract on the Data Source page and configure the extract before saving it.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For a physical join, drag the first table to the canvas, double-click it, and then drag the second table into the join canvas. In the join dialog, choose the join type and matching fields. If the question requires all customers, place and preserve the named side appropriately; inner keeps matches, left or right preserves its named side, and full outer preserves both.

If the workflow uses an extract, select Extract on the Data Source page and configure it before saving. An extract is a saved snapshot for analysis, not a claim that it always shows the newest source state.

The useful output is a connection and prepared data arrangement suited to the reporting question. Keep the physical-join canvas step explicit: dragging tables without explaining the double-click entry to that canvas leaves a beginner without the named workflow. The example ends at preparation, not at worksheet charts or dashboard placement.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: An extract is a saved snapshot, so do not describe it as inherently live. Also preserve the distinction between connecting, creating a physical join in its canvas, and selecting an extract. Those are different preparation choices and actions.

practice_anchor.objective: Connect Tableau to the supplied Customers and Orders source using the appropriate connector and source-specific information. required_facts.statement: A current-state assessment describes the present situation as a baseline for identifying improvements.
Record detailed notes about the current business situation in a structured current-state column.
Organize the current-state notes by the business areas being assessed so they can be compared with goals and gaps.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/gap-analysis — Categorize information and start your analysis; Assess current state

text.content: Imagine an operations team wants to improve dispatch preparation. Before defining the desired result, record the present situation as a baseline. In this hypothetical assessment, dispatch information is kept in separate records, clarification calls occur before preparation, and one branch uses a different handoff from another.

text.title: Current-State Capability Assessment
text.content: A current-state assessment describes the present situation as a baseline for identifying improvements.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Record detailed notes about the current business situation in a structured current-state column. Organize the current-state notes by the business areas being assessed so they can be compared with goals and gaps.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Put detailed current-state notes in a structured current-state column. Organize them by business area: instruction access, handoffs, and dispatch preparation. That organization makes later comparison possible without mixing every observation into one vague statement such as “the process is inefficient.”

For instruction access, the example note might be “Staff consult a separate sheet for current instructions.” For handoffs, it might describe who supplies amended information. If the scenario provides a measured preparation time, record it with its context. Do not invent a baseline number merely because a later target will need comparison.

The output is a description of the present business situation arranged by the areas being assessed. It is not yet a list of desired changes. Keep an observed condition, a proposed improvement, and a judgment about success separate. This way a reader can see what current situation the subsequent goals and gaps refer to, rather than having to reconstruct the baseline from the recommendation.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Current-state assessment is not a wish list. A note saying “use one instruction record” describes a desired change, not the current situation. Record the baseline in the current-state column and organize it by the assessed business areas.

practice_anchor.objective: Write a current-state capability assessment for the supplied hypothetical dispatch situation in a table with Business area and Current state columns. Organize detailed baseline notes under instruction access, handoffs, and dispatch preparation.
practice_anchor.success: Each business area has current-state notes grounded in the supplied situation. The notes describe present conditions rather than desired changes, retain any supplied measurement context without inventing numbers, and provide an organized baseline for later comparison with goals and gaps.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make visible a two-column assessment organized by instruction access, handoffs, and dispatch preparation. Annotate the Current state column to show detailed present-condition notes, distinguish them from desired changes, and explain how grouping notes by business area supports later comparison.

notes: Stay with structured baseline notes; do not assume measurements absent from the situation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A desired-state definition states the objectives and situation the business wants to achieve.
Express the goal using a business outcome and measurable success target.
Write the desired objectives alongside the corresponding business areas in the desired-state column.

text.content: Suppose the current-state assessment records lengthy dispatch preparation and unclear instruction access. Future-state vision states the objectives and situation the business wants to achieve, with a business outcome and measurable success target.

text.title: Future-State Vision Definition
text.content: A desired-state definition states the objectives and situation the business wants to achieve.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Express the goal using a business outcome and measurable success target. Write the desired objectives alongside the corresponding business areas in the desired-state column.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical effort, a desired objective could be “Dispatch staff prepare orders with current instructions, with preparation completed within five minutes in the stated operating conditions.” The five-minute target is an example business decision, not a standard for every dispatch operation. It gives the desired state more substance than “make dispatch better.”

Write desired objectives in the desired-state column beside the corresponding business areas. The instruction-access objective belongs alongside the instruction-access baseline; the preparation target belongs alongside the preparation baseline. Keeping that alignment visible lets readers compare like areas rather than comparing a broad aspiration with an unrelated current note.

The useful output is a future situation described in terms of business outcome and success target. It does not need to name a particular tool as the vision. “Purchase software” states an action, while “staff have current instructions and meet the preparation target” describes what the business wants to achieve. Keep the target’s conditions visible so its meaning is not lost in a slogan.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A future-state vision is not merely a named solution or a favorable adjective. State the desired business outcome with a measurable success target. It is intended future behavior, not evidence that the business has already reached that state.

practice_anchor.objective: For the hypothetical dispatch effort, write a future-state vision describing staff preparing orders with current instructions and completing preparation within five minutes under the stated operating conditions. Enter the desired objectives in the desired-state column beside the corresponding instruction-access and preparation business areas; no formulas are needed.
practice_anchor.success: The statement describes the intended business situation rather than a tool purchase, includes the five-minute preparation target with its operating conditions, and places each desired objective beside its corresponding business area. The target is treated as a decision for this hypothetical effort, not a universal standard.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show instruction access and dispatch preparation as separate business-area rows, with current-state notes and aligned desired-state objectives. Annotate the desired objectives to distinguish the business outcome from the measurable preparation target and its stated operating conditions.

notes: Do not turn the desired target into an unsupported universal service level.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A gap is a specific difference between the current situation and the desired state.
Compare the current-state description with the desired-state objectives and list the specific differences keeping the business from those goals.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/gap-analysis — Assess current state; Define the desired state; Identify gaps

text.content: Imagine the current-state column says dispatch preparation takes twelve minutes under the assessed conditions, while the desired-state column sets a five-minute target under the same conditions. The specific time difference is seven minutes. Another current note says staff consult two instruction sources, while the desired state calls for current instructions available in one place.

text.title: Gap Identification and Analysis
text.content: A gap is a specific difference between the current situation and the desired state.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Compare the current-state description with the desired-state objectives and list the specific differences keeping the business from those goals.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Compare each current description with its corresponding desired objective. List the specific differences keeping the business from the goal: the preparation-time difference and the information-access difference in this hypothetical case. These are more precise than writing only “there is a dispatch gap.”

Keep the comparison tied to the descriptions supplied. If the current-state record contains no preparation-time measurement, do not calculate a numerical difference by inventing one. You can still identify the documented qualitative difference and preserve any missing information as a question.

The output is a gap list grounded in current and desired states. It does not itself prove the cause of every gap or choose the solution. The immediate analytical task is to make the difference explicit enough that stakeholders can see what has to change. The example’s numbers and one-place objective illustrate that comparison, not a claim about a real organization.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A gap is the difference between current and desired states, not simply a complaint or a proposed fix. “Buy a new system” does not identify the difference. Compare corresponding descriptions and state what separates the business from its goal.

practice_anchor.objective: Compare the supplied current- and desired-state descriptions for dispatch preparation and select the concrete differences to include in a gap list.
practice_anchor.success: The gap list identifies the seven-minute preparation-time difference and the difference between consulting two instruction sources and having current instructions available in one place, without substituting a complaint, inferred cause, or proposed fix.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show aligned current-state, desired-state, and specific-gap columns for the hypothetical dispatch example: twelve versus five minutes gives a seven-minute difference; two instruction sources versus current instructions in one place gives an information-access difference.

notes: Do not infer root causes or guaranteed solutions from a gap alone.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: SWOT separates strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats in a business situation.
Strengths are internal advantages; weaknesses are internal limitations.
Opportunities are favorable external possibilities; threats are external factors that could harm success.
Create four labeled quadrants and place each factor according to whether it is internal or external and favorable or unfavorable.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/strategic-planning/swot-analysis — How to conduct a SWOT analysis

text.content: Suppose an order-service team is assessing a business situation. Its experienced dispatch staff are an internal advantage, while fragmented instruction records are an internal limitation. A new external delivery partnership may create a favorable possibility, while an external competitor’s improved service may threaten success.

text.title: SWOT Analysis
text.content: SWOT separates strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats in a business situation.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Strengths are internal advantages; weaknesses are internal limitations. Opportunities are favorable external possibilities; threats are external factors that could harm success. Create four labeled quadrants and place each factor according to whether it is internal or external and favorable or unfavorable.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Create four labeled quadrants: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats. Place experienced staff under Strengths and fragmented records under Weaknesses. Place the partnership possibility under Opportunities and the competitor factor under Threats. These are hypothetical factors selected to make the two distinctions clear.

For each placement, ask two questions: is the factor internal or external, and favorable or unfavorable? Strong staff and the partnership are both favorable, but one is internal and the other external. Fragmentation and the competitor factor are both unfavorable, but they also belong on different sides of that distinction.

The useful result is an organized view of the situation rather than an unclassified list of positive and negative comments. Do not classify solely by whether a factor sounds important. A favorable external possibility belongs under Opportunities even if the team hopes to benefit from it internally. Keep the classification tied to the factor being described.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Strengths and opportunities are not interchangeable synonyms for positives; internal versus external distinguishes them. The same distinction separates weaknesses from threats. A four-quadrant layout helps only when each factor is placed using both dimensions.

practice_anchor.objective: Build a four-quadrant SWOT matrix for the hypothetical order-service team by placing experienced dispatch staff, fragmented instruction records, a possible external delivery partnership, and an external competitor’s improved service into the labeled quadrants.
practice_anchor.success: The matrix has Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats quadrants. Experienced dispatch staff are placed under Strengths, fragmented instruction records under Weaknesses, the possible external delivery partnership under Opportunities, and the competitor’s improved service under Threats, using both internal versus external and favorable versus unfavorable distinctions.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a four-quadrant SWOT matrix with Strengths and Weaknesses identified as internal, Opportunities and Threats as external, and the favorable versus unfavorable distinction visible. Place each of the four order-service factors in its corresponding quadrant.

notes: Avoid scoring SWOT factors or implying SWOT proves causation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: MoSCoW groups requirements as Must have, Should have, Could have, or Will not have for the scope being prioritized.
Must-have items are essential: without them the solution would not work or the project would be useless.
Should-have items are important but the solution can still work without them.
Could-have items are desirable but nonessential and have a smaller impact if omitted.
Will-not-have items are not needed within the prioritization scope and can be deprioritized or dropped.
Define the prioritization scope, discuss each item’s importance, and assign the category the group agrees fits it.

text.content: Imagine prioritizing requirements for an initial delivery-instruction release. Define that scope before assigning MoSCoW categories. In this hypothetical scope, seeing current instructions is essential: without it, the solution would not work for its stated purpose, so the group assigns Must have.

text.title: MoSCoW Prioritization
text.content: MoSCoW groups requirements as Must have, Should have, Could have, or Will not have for the scope being prioritized.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Must-have items are essential: without them the solution would not work or the project would be useless. Should-have items are important but the solution can still work without them. Could-have items are desirable but nonessential and have a smaller impact if omitted. Will-not-have items are not needed within the prioritization scope and can be deprioritized or dropped. Define the prioritization scope, discuss each item’s importance, and assign the category the group agrees fits it.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
An amendment indicator is important but the solution can still work without it, so it is a Should have in this example. A convenience color choice is desirable, nonessential, and has a smaller omission impact, so it is a Could have. A vehicle-purchasing feature is not needed within this scope, so it is Will not have. The same labels are not universal classifications of those features; they depend on the agreed scope and importance.

Discuss each item’s importance and assign the category the group agrees fits. Keep the reasoning attached to the category so Must have is not simply a synonym for “a stakeholder wants it strongly.” Should have and Could have both allow a working solution without the item, but the described importance and omission impact differ.

The practical output is scope-specific grouping that distinguishes essential work from important, desirable, or excluded work. Will not have refers to what is not needed within the prioritization scope; it need not be rewritten as a claim that the organization must never consider that item.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: MoSCoW categories are not just four levels of enthusiasm. Must have is essential to a working or useful solution in the stated scope. Will not have is scope-specific, not necessarily a permanent ban. Define the scope and discuss importance before assigning labels.

practice_anchor.objective: Categorize eight given requirements for the hypothetical initial delivery-instruction release as Must have, Should have, Could have, or Will not have. Use the stated scope and each requirement's importance and omission impact to justify each assignment.
practice_anchor.success: All eight requirements receive categories consistent with the stated scope and supplied importance information. Justifications distinguish essential requirements from important but nonessential requirements, lower-impact desirable requirements, and requirements not needed within scope.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the agreed initial delivery-instruction release scope visible above an annotated table linking current instructions, an amendment indicator, a convenience color choice, and a vehicle-purchasing feature to their respective MoSCoW categories and scope-specific reasons.

notes: Keep “Will not have” terminology from the brief; no unsupported percentage allocations.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Kano classifies features by how functionality relates to customer satisfaction.
Must-be or basic features are expected; their absence causes dissatisfaction, while their presence adds little satisfaction.
Performance features produce more satisfaction as their functionality improves.
Attractive or excitement features can delight users who did not expect them and may not notice their absence.
Use user evidence about satisfaction and the feature’s functionality to classify and discuss the appropriate category.
Indifferent features are those users feel neutral toward: changes in their functionality do not significantly increase or decrease customer satisfaction.

text.content: Suppose user evidence about an order service shows several different satisfaction patterns. Users expect their current instructions to be accurate and are dissatisfied when they are missing; providing them adds little extra satisfaction. That pattern fits a Must-be or basic feature.

text.title: Kano Analysis
text.content: Kano classifies features by how functionality relates to customer satisfaction.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Must-be or basic features are expected; their absence causes dissatisfaction, while their presence adds little satisfaction. Performance features produce more satisfaction as their functionality improves. Attractive or excitement features can delight users who did not expect them and may not notice their absence. Use user evidence about satisfaction and the feature’s functionality to classify and discuss the appropriate category. Indifferent features are those users feel neutral toward: changes in their functionality do not significantly increase or decrease customer satisfaction.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Evidence might show that progressively quicker instruction access produces more satisfaction: that is a Performance pattern. An unexpected helpful suggestion could delight users while its absence goes unnoticed: that is an Attractive or excitement pattern. If users remain neutral as a feature’s functionality changes, it is Indifferent.

Classify using evidence about satisfaction and functionality, not the BA’s personal excitement about an idea. In this hypothetical case, the same design team might find a decorative feature exciting while user evidence shows neutrality. The evidence would support Indifferent rather than Attractive.

The useful output is a discussion of how functionality relates to satisfaction. These categories do not state delivery priority by themselves. A feature being expected is a satisfaction pattern, while a separate prioritization decision asks what belongs in the delivery scope.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Attractive means it can delight users who did not expect it; it does not mean the team likes the feature. Basic features can cause dissatisfaction when absent even though their presence adds little satisfaction. Preserve that asymmetry instead of treating all features as linear satisfaction gains.

practice_anchor.objective: Classify five given features of the hypothetical order service as Must-be/basic, Performance, Attractive/excitement, or Indifferent, using supplied user evidence about functionality and satisfaction. Provide a justification for each classification.
practice_anchor.success: All five features are matched to the category supported by the supplied evidence. Each justification explains the relevant satisfaction pattern: dissatisfaction when an expected feature is absent, increasing satisfaction as functionality improves, unexpected delight with little response to absence, or neutrality as functionality changes.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the four Kano satisfaction patterns visible side by side, contrasting user responses when functionality is absent, present, or improved. Label Must-be/basic, Performance, Attractive/excitement, and Indifferent, and connect each pattern to user evidence from the hypothetical order service.

notes: Include Indifferent; avoid adding unsupported Kano categories or survey procedures.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.
